Lessons.Title: Same Denominator or Numerator
ExplanationParagraphs: Original 2021 IM Grade4 Unit2 Lesson3; source teacher lesson and Student Task Statements 4-page PDF reviewed locally. Use same-sized fraction strips for same-numerator/denominator comparisons.
Warm-up Number Talk: 136+100=236,136+300=436,136+370=506,136+378=514. Discuss different mental addition strategies.
Activity1 source five same-denominator pairs: 3/4 vs5/4;3/5 vs5/5;3/6 vs5/6;3/8 vs5/8;3/10 vs5/10. Each 5/d greater. Label strips with1,2,3,4,5,6,8 equal parts; explain 10/3>7/3 even when improper.

Activity2 source five same-numerator pairs:1/3 vs1/5;2/3 vs2/5;3/3 vs3/5;4/3 vs4/5;9/3 vs9/5. Each n/3 greater; compare70/20>70/100; explain why Tyler's4/10>4/6 assertion is false. Structured partner discussion and revised written reasoning are teacher-reviewed.

Lesson synthesis: same denominator → bigger numerator; same numerator → smaller denominator, for equal-size wholes. Original source mathematical conversations must not be represented as automatically graded.
Edulytics independently authored 5-minute Cool-down (NOT publisher-original): explain why5/8>3/8 and4/6>4/10 using unit-piece language and a diagram. Teacher checks open reasoning.

KeyConcepts.Title: Equal numerators
KeyConcepts.Definition: Same number of parts of different sizes.

WorkedExamples.Title: Tyler misconception
WorkedExamples.Question: Is4/10 greater than4/6?
Steps: A tenth is smaller than a sixth.
Four tenths covers less than four sixths.

WorkedExamples.Title: Independently authored Grade 4 lesson reasoning
WorkedExamples.Question: Which is greater, 3/7 or 5/7?
WorkedExamples.Method: Use the exact relationship and representation requested by this lesson.
Steps: Both numbers refer to the same whole partitioned into seven equal pieces.
Compare the numerators: five pieces exceed three.
Their difference is 2/7 of that whole.
WorkedExamples.Check: First-party mathematically checked model. Original publisher activity and student drawings require independent teacher review.

CommonMistakes.Mistake: Bigger denominator always means bigger value.
CommonMistakes.WhyWrong: It makes each equal-whole unit piece smaller.

CommonMistakes.Mistake: Comparing only denominators and ignoring the numerator.
CommonMistakes.WhyWrong: Equal denominators mean each piece has equal size; count the pieces.
CommonMistakes.Correction: Equal denominators mean each piece has equal size; count the pieces.

SummaryPoints: All original5 same-denominator pairs, 5 same-numerator pairs, two improper comparisons and Tyler correction preserved.
Original Number Talk and teacher-reviewed source strip diagrams retained.
